segment.text: 笆に媚ぶる野萩の下露もはや秋の色なり。人々は争うて帰りを急ぎぬ。小松の温泉に景勝の第一を占めて、さしも賑わい合えりし梅屋の上も下も、尾越しに通う鹿笛の音に哀れを誘われて、廊下を行き交う足音もやや淋しくなりぬ。車のあとより車の多くは旅鞄と客とを載せて、一里先なる停車場を指して走りぬ。膳の通い茶の通いに、久しく馴れ睦みたる婢どもは、さすがに後影を見送りてしばし佇立めり。前を遶る渓河の水は、淙々として遠く流れ行く。かなたの森に鳴くは鶇か。
segment.source: 笆《まがき》に媚《こ》ぶる野萩《のはぎ》の下露もはや秋の色なり。人々は争うて帰りを急ぎぬ。小松の温泉《いでゆ》に景勝の第一を占めて、さしも賑《にぎ》わい合えりし梅屋の上も下も、尾越しに通う鹿笛《しかぶえ》の音《ね》に哀れを誘われて、廊下を行《ゆ》き交《か》う足音もやや淋《さび》しくなりぬ。車のあとより車の多くは旅鞄《たびかばん》と客とを載せて、一里先なる停車場《すていしょん》を指して走りぬ。膳《ぜん》の通い茶の通いに、久しく馴《な》れ睦《むつ》みたる婢《おんな》どもは、さすがに後影を見送りてしばし佇立《たたず》めり。前を遶《めぐ》る渓河《たにがわ》の水は、淙々《そうそう》として遠く流れ行く。かなたの森に鳴くは鶇《つぐみ》か。

sentences.text: 笆に媚ぶる野萩の下露もはや秋の色なり。
人々は争うて帰りを急ぎぬ。
小松の温泉に景勝の第一を占めて、さしも賑わい合えりし梅屋の上も下も、尾越しに通う鹿笛の音に哀れを誘われて、廊下を行き交う足音もやや淋しくなりぬ。
車のあとより車の多くは旅鞄と客とを載せて、一里先なる停車場を指して走りぬ。
膳の通い茶の通いに、久しく馴れ睦みたる婢どもは、さすがに後影を見送りてしばし佇立めり。
前を遶る渓河の水は、淙々として遠く流れ行く。
かなたの森に鳴くは鶇か。

segment.text: 朝夕のたつきも知らざりし山中も、年々の避暑の客に思わぬ煙を増して、瓦葺きの家も木の葉越しにところどころ見ゆ。尾上に雲あり、ひときわ高き松が根に起りて、巌にからむ蔦の上にたなびけり。立ち続く峰々は市ある里の空を隠して、争い落つる滝の千筋はさながら銀糸を振り乱しぬ。北は見渡す限り目も藐に、鹿垣きびしく鳴子は遠く連なりて、山田の秋も忙がしげなり。西ははるかに水の行衛を見せて、山幾重雲幾重、鳥は高く飛びて木の葉はおのずから翻りぬ。草苅りの子の一人二人、心豊かに馬を歩ませて、節面白く唄い連れたるが、今しも端山の裾を登り行きぬ。
segment.source: 朝夕のたつきも知らざりし山中《やまなか》も、年々の避暑の客に思わぬ煙《けぶり》を増して、瓦葺《かわらぶ》きの家《や》も木の葉越しにところどころ見ゆ。尾上《おのえ》に雲あり、ひときわ高き松が根に起りて、巌《いわお》にからむ蔦《つた》の上にたなびけり。立ち続く峰々は市《いち》ある里の空を隠して、争い落つる滝の千筋《ちすじ》はさながら銀糸を振り乱しぬ。北は見渡す限り目も藐《はる》に、鹿垣《ししがき》きびしく鳴子《なるこ》は遠く連なりて、山田の秋も忙がしげなり。西ははるかに水の行衛《ゆくえ》を見せて、山幾重雲幾重、鳥は高く飛びて木の葉はおのずから翻りぬ。草苅《くさか》りの子の一人二人、心豊かに馬を歩ませて、節面白く唄《うた》い連れたるが、今しも端山《はやま》の裾《すそ》を登り行きぬ。

sentences.text: 朝夕のたつきも知らざりし山中も、年々の避暑の客に思わぬ煙を増して、瓦葺きの家も木の葉越しにところどころ見ゆ。
尾上に雲あり、ひときわ高き松が根に起りて、巌にからむ蔦の上にたなびけり。
立ち続く峰々は市ある里の空を隠して、争い落つる滝の千筋はさながら銀糸を振り乱しぬ。
北は見渡す限り目も藐に、鹿垣きびしく鳴子は遠く連なりて、山田の秋も忙がしげなり。
西ははるかに水の行衛を見せて、山幾重雲幾重、鳥は高く飛びて木の葉はおのずから翻りぬ。
草苅りの子の一人二人、心豊かに馬を歩ませて、節面白く唄い連れたるが、今しも端山の裾を登り行きぬ。

segment.text: 荻の湖の波はいと静かなり。嵐の誘う木葉舟の、島隠れ行く影もほの見ゆ。折しも松の風を払って、妙なる琴の音は二階の一間に起りぬ。新たに来たる離座敷の客は耳を傾けつ。
segment.source: 荻《おぎ》の湖《こ》の波はいと静かなり。嵐《あらし》の誘う木葉舟の、島隠れ行く影もほの見ゆ。折しも松の風を払って、妙《たえ》なる琴の音は二階の一間に起りぬ。新たに来たる離座敷《はなれ》の客は耳を傾《かたぶ》けつ。

sentences.text: 荻の湖の波はいと静かなり。
嵐の誘う木葉舟の、島隠れ行く影もほの見ゆ。
折しも松の風を払って、妙なる琴の音は二階の一間に起りぬ。
新たに来たる離座敷の客は耳を傾けつ。

segment.text: 糸につれて唄い出す声は、岩間に咽ぶ水を抑えて、巧みに流す生田の一節、客はまたさらに心を動かしてか、煙草をよそに思わずそなたを見上げぬ。障子は隔ての関を据えて、松は心なく光琳風の影を宿せり。客はそのまま目を転じて、下の谷間を打ち見やりしが、耳はなお曲に惹かるるごとく、髭を撚りて身動きもせず。玉は乱れ落ちてにわかに繁き琴の手は、再び流れて清く滑らかなる声は次いで起れり。客はまたもそなたを見上げぬ。

segment.text: 廊下を通う婢を呼び止めて、唄の主は誰と聞けば、顔を見て異しく笑う。さては大方美しき人なるべし。何者と重ねて問えば、私は存じませぬとばかり、はや岡焼きの色を見せて、溜室の方へと走り行きぬ。定めて朋輩の誰彼に、それと噂の種なるべし。客は微笑みて後を見送りしが、水に臨める縁先に立ち出でて、傍の椅子に身を寄せ掛けぬ。琴の主はなお惜しげもなく美しき声を送れり。
segment.source: 廊下を通う婢《おんな》を呼び止めて、唄の主は誰《たれ》と聞けば、顔を見て異《おか》しく笑う。さては大方美しき人なるべし。何者と重ねて問えば、私は存じませぬとばかり、はや岡焼《おかや》きの色を見せて、溜室《たまり》の方へと走り行きぬ。定めて朋輩《ほうばい》の誰彼に、それと噂《うわさ》の種なるべし。客は微笑《ほほえ》みて後を見送りしが、水に臨める縁先に立ち出《い》でて、傍《かたえ》の椅子《いす》に身を寄せ掛けぬ。琴の主はなお惜しげもなく美しき声を送れり。

segment.text: 客はさる省の書記官に、奥村辰弥とて売出しの男、はからぬ病に公の暇を乞い、ようやく本に復したる後の身を養わんとて、今日しもこの梅屋に来たれるなり。燦爛かなる扮装と見事なる髭とは、帳場より亭主を飛び出さして、恭しき辞儀の下より最も眺望に富みたるこの離座敷に通されぬ。三十前後の顔はそれよりも更けたるが、鋭き眼の中に言われぬ愛敬のあるを、客擦れたる婢の一人は見つけ出して口々に友の弄りものとなりぬ。辰弥は生得馴るるに早く、咄嗟の間に気の置かれぬお方様となれり。過分の茶代に度を失いたる亭主は、急ぎ衣裳を改めて御挨拶に罷り出でしが、書記官様と聞くよりなお一層敬い奉りぬ。
segment.source: 客はさる省の書記官に、奥村｜辰弥《たつや》とて売出しの男、はからぬ病に公の暇を乞《こ》い、ようやく本に復したる後の身を養わんとて、今日しもこの梅屋に来たれるなり。燦爛《きらびや》かなる扮装《いでたち》と見事なる髭《ひげ》とは、帳場より亭主を飛び出さして、恭《うやうや》しき辞儀の下より最も眺望《ちょうぼう》に富みたるこの離座敷《はなれ》に通されぬ。三十前後の顔はそれよりも更《ふ》けたるが、鋭き眼の中《うち》に言われぬ愛敬《あいきょう》のあるを、客｜擦《ず》れたる婢《おんな》の一人は見つけ出して口々に友の弄《なぶ》りものとなりぬ。辰弥は生得馴るるに早く、咄嗟《とっさ》の間に気の置かれぬお方様となれり。過分の茶代に度を失いたる亭主は、急ぎ衣裳《いしょう》を改めて御挨拶《ごあいさつ》に罷《まか》り出でしが、書記官様と聞くよりなお一層敬い奉りぬ。

sentences.text: 客はさる省の書記官に、奥村辰弥とて売出しの男、はからぬ病に公の暇を乞い、ようやく本に復したる後の身を養わんとて、今日しもこの梅屋に来たれるなり。
燦爛かなる扮装と見事なる髭とは、帳場より亭主を飛び出さして、恭しき辞儀の下より最も眺望に富みたるこの離座敷に通されぬ。
三十前後の顔はそれよりも更けたるが、鋭き眼の中に言われぬ愛敬のあるを、客擦れたる婢の一人は見つけ出して口々に友の弄りものとなりぬ。
辰弥は生得馴るるに早く、咄嗟の間に気の置かれぬお方様となれり。
過分の茶代に度を失いたる亭主は、急ぎ衣裳を改めて御挨拶に罷り出でしが、書記官様と聞くよりなお一層敬い奉りぬ。

segment.text: 琴はやがて曲を終りて、静かに打ち語らう声のたしかならず聞ゆ。辰弥も今は相対う風色に見入りて、心は早やそこにあらず。折しも障子はさっと開きて、中なる人は立ち出でたるがごとし。辰弥の耳は逸早く聞きつけて振り返りぬ。欄干にあらわれたるは五十路に近き満丸顔の、打見にも元気よき老人なり。骨も埋もるるばかり肥え太りて、角袖着せたる布袋をそのまま、笑ましげに障子の中へ振り向きしが、話しかくる一言の末に身を反らせて打ち笑いぬ。中なる人の影は見えず。

segment.text: 半日の囲碁に互いの胸を開きて、善平はことに辰弥を得たるを喜びぬ。何省書記官正何位という幾字は、昔気質の耳に立ち優れてよく響き渡り、かかる人に親しく語らうを身の面目とすれば、訪われたるあとよりすぐに訪い返して、ひたすらになお睦まじからんことを願えり。才物だ。なかなかの才物だとしきりに誉め称やし、あの高ぶらぬところがどうも豪い。談話の面白さ。人接のよさと一々に感服したる末は、何として、綱雄などのなかなか及ぶところでないと独り語つ。光代は傍に聞いていたりしが、それでもあの綱雄さんは、もっと若くって上品で、沈着いていて気性が高くって、あの方よりはよッぽどようござんすわ。と調子に確かめて膝押し進む。ホイ、お前の前で言うのではなかった。と善平は笑い出せば、あら、そういうわけで言ったのではありませぬ。ただこうだと言って見たばかりですよ。と顔は早くも淡紅を散らして、いやな父様だよ。と帯締めの打紐を解きつ結びつ。
segment.source: 半日の囲碁に互いの胸を開きて、善平はことに辰弥を得たるを喜びぬ。何省書記官正何位という幾字は、昔気質《むかしかたぎ》の耳に立ち優れてよく響き渡り、かかる人に親しく語らうを身の面目とすれば、訪《と》われたるあとよりすぐに訪い返して、ひたすらになお睦《むつ》まじからんことを願えり。才物だ。なかなかの才物だとしきりに誉《ほ》め称《そ》やし、あの高ぶらぬところがどうも豪《えら》い。談話《はなし》の面白さ。人接《ひとづき》のよさと一々に感服したる末は、何として、綱雄《つなお》などのなかなか及ぶところでないと独《ひと》り語《ご》つ。光代は傍に聞いていたりしが、それでもあの綱雄さんは、もっと若くって上品で、沈着《おちつ》いていて気性が高くって、あの方よりはよッぽどようござんすわ。と調子に確かめて膝《ひざ》押し進む。ホイ、お前の前で言うのではなかった。と善平は笑い出せば、あら、そういうわけで言ったのではありませぬ。ただこうだと言って見たばかりですよ。と顔は早くも淡紅《うすくれない》を散らして、いやな父様だよ。と帯締めの打紐《うちひも》を解きつ結びつ。

segment.text: 光代は向き直りて、父様はなぜそう奥村さんを御贔負になさるの。と不平らしく顔を見る。なぜとはどういう心だ。誉めていいから誉めるのではないか。と父親は煙草を払く。それだっても、他人ではありませぬか。と思いありげなる娘の顔。うむ、分った。綱雄を贔負せぬのが気に入らぬというのか。なるほどそれは御もっともの次第だ。いやもう綱雄は見上げた男さ。お前のいう通り若くて上品で、それから何だッけな、うむその沈着いていて気性が高くて、まだ入用ならば学問が深くて腕が確かで男前がよくて品行が正しくて、ああ疲労れた、どこに一箇所落ちというものがない若者だ。

松が小島、離れ岩、山は浮世を隔てて水は長えに清く、漁唱菱歌、煙波縹緲として空はさらに悠なり。
倒れたる木に腰打ち掛けて光代はしばらく休らいぬ。
風は粉膩を撲ってなまめかしき香を辰弥に送れり。

segment.text: 参りましょう。親父ももう帰って来る時分でございます。と光代は立ち上りぬ。ここらはゆッくり休むところもなくっていけませんな。と辰弥もついにまたの折を期しぬ。道すがらも辰弥はさまざまに話しかけしが、光代はただかたばかりの返事のみして、深くは心を留めぬさまなり。見るから辰弥も気に染まず、さすが思いに沈むもののごとし。二人は黙して歩みぬ。

segment.text: これは私の親戚のもので、東条綱雄と申すものです。と善平に紹介されたる辰弥は、例の隔てなき挨拶をせしが、心の中は穏やかならず。この蒼白き、仔細らしき、あやしき男はそもそも何者ぞ。光代の振舞いのなお心得ぬ。あるいは、とばかり疑いしが、色にも見せずあくまで快げに装いぬ。傲然として鼻の先にあしらうごとき綱雄の仕打ちには、幾たびか心を傷つけられながらも、人慣れたる身はさりげなく打ち笑えど、綱雄はさらに取り合う気色もなく、光代、お前に買って来た土産があるが、何だと思う。当てて見んか。と見向きもやらず。

と思わぬ飛〓に口をつぐむ途端、辰弥よりの使いは急がわしく来たりて言われたる通りの口上を述べぬ。
半ばは意気張りずくの善平は二つ返事に、承知の由を答えて帰しぬ。
綱雄は腕を組んで差し俯向けり。

segment.text: 光代は気遣わしげに二人を見かわせしが、そのまま立ち上る父を止めて、父様、それではお互いに心持がよくないではありませんか。何とか仲を直しておいでなさいな。私は困るわ。

segment.text: 何事か起りたるとは知らぬにあらねど、光代は差し当りての身の物憂げなるを、慰めてくれぬ父を恨めしと思いぬ。憂いに重ぬる不満は穂にあらわれて、父様、つまりませぬから私も帰りまする。と辛きに当てて不興らしく言う。善平はさらに耳にも入れず、何にしてもかの炭山が手に入れば、例の失策の株以来、手ひどく受けた痛みもすッかり療治が出来る。その上日清事件の影響から、海産物に及ぼした損失もこれで埋合せがつくというもの。いや首尾よくやって見たいものだ。とわれを忘れて調子づく。

segment.text: 父様、父様ッたらば父様、私は帰りますよ。と光代は声を励ましていとどけわしく言う。善平は初めて心づきたるごとく、なに帰る？　私も帰るさ。一時も早く東京へ帰って、何彼の手はずを極めねばならぬ。光代、明日ははやく発とうぞ。それにしても炭山は、ぜひとも手に入れたいものだ。と半ばは先に心を奪わる。

segment.text: その日よりして三好の家に辰弥の往復は磯打つ波のひまなくなりぬ。善平との間はさながら親戚のごとくなれり。家内の皆々は辰弥のこのたびの事件に重なる人なることを知りぬ。先に立つ善平につれて誰も彼も疎略には思わざりき。辰弥は思うがままに蜘蛛の糸を吐きかけて人々をことごとく網の中につつみぬ。かくして末の婢より上の隠居に至るまで、辰弥は親しき中の親しき人となりぬ。三好の家と辰弥とは、ようやく離るべからざるものとなれり。中に立って光代は独り打ち腹立ちぬ。見るほど何ゆえとも知らねどいよいよ疎ましき辰弥に、かくまで語らい寄る父の恨めしく、隔意を置かぬ母の口惜しく、心やすげなる姉の憎く、笑顔を見する兄の喰いつきてもやりたく、三方四方面白くなくて面白くなくて、果ては焦れ出す疳癪に、当り散らさるる仲働きの婢は途方に暮れて、何とせんかと泣き顔の浮世のさまはただ不思議なり。光代は一筋に綱雄を待ちぬ。他の気も知らず綱雄はいつまでも帰り来たらず。光代は一人物憂げに朝夕の雲を望めり。指して定まらぬ行衛に結ぼるる胸はいよいよ苦しく、今ごろはどこにどうしてかと、打ち向う鏡は窶れを見せて、それもいつしか太息に曇りぬ。

segment.text: 善平は見もやらず心もそぞろに、今日はまた珍客の入来とて、朝まだきの床の中より用意に急がしく、それ庭を掃け裀を出せ、銀穂屋付きの手炉に、一閑釣瓶の煙草盆、床には御自慢の探幽が、和歌の三夕これを見てくれの三幅対、銘も聞けがし宗甫作の花入れに、野山の錦の秋を見せて、あわれ心を筑紫潟、浪に千鳥の蒔絵盆には、鎌倉時代と伝えたる金溜塗りの重香合、碪手青磁の香炉に添えて、銀葉挾みの手の内に、霞を分けて入る柴舟の、行衛は煙の末にも知れと、しばしば心にうなずくなるべし。脇には七宝入りの紫檀卓に、銀蒼鷹の置物を据えて、これも談話の数に入れとや、極彩色の金屏風は、手を尽したる光琳が花鳥の盛上げ、あっぱれ座敷や高麗縁の青畳に、玉を置くとも羞かしからぬ設けの席より、前は茶庭の十分なる侘びを見せて、目移りゆかしくここを価値の買いどころと、客より先に主人の満足は、顔に横撫での煤を付けながら、独り妙と隈なく八方を見廻しぬ。
segment.source: 善平は見もやらず心もそぞろに、今日はまた珍客の入来《じゅらい》とて、朝まだきの床の中より用意に急がしく、それ庭を掃け※［＃「ころもへん＋因」、第4水準2-88-18］《しとね》を出せ、銀穂屋《ぎんぼや》付きの手炉《てあぶり》に、一閑釣瓶《いっかんつるべ》の煙草盆、床には御自慢の探幽《たんゆう》が、和歌の三夕これを見てくれの三幅対、銘も聞けがし宗甫《そうほ》作の花入れに、野山の錦の秋を見せて、あわれ心を筑紫潟《つくしがた》、浪に千鳥の蒔絵盆《まきえぼん》には、鎌倉時代と伝えたる金溜塗《きんためぬ》りの重香合《じゅうこうごう》、碪手青磁《きぬたでせいじ》の香炉に添えて、銀葉挾《ぎんようばさ》みの手の内に、霞《かすみ》を分けて入る柴舟《しばふね》の、行衛は煙《けぶり》の末にも知れと、しばしば心にうなずくなるべし。脇《わき》には七宝入りの紫檀《したん》卓に、銀蒼鷹《ぎんくまたか》の置物を据《す》えて、これも談話《はなし》の数に入れとや、極彩色の金屏風《きんびょうぶ》は、手を尽したる光琳《こうりん》が花鳥の盛上げ、あっぱれ座敷や高麗縁《こうらいべり》の青畳に、玉を置くとも羞かしからぬ設けの席より、前は茶庭の十分なる侘《わ》びを見せて、目移りゆかしくここを価値《ねうち》の買いどころと、客より先に主人の満足は、顔に横撫での煤《すす》を付けながら、独り妙《みょう》と隈《くま》なく八方を見廻しぬ。

segment.text: ほどもなく入り来る洋服扮装の七分は髯黒の客人、座敷に入りてしばらくは打ち潜めきたる密議に移りしが、やがて開きて二側に居流れたるを合図として、運び出づる杯盤の料理は善四郎が念入りの庖丁、献酬いまだ半ばならず早くも笑いさざめく声々を、よそに聞きて光代は口惜しげに涙ぐみぬ。座敷の急がしさに取り紛れて誰一人ここを訪わんとせざるも、女心には恨みの一つなり。

segment.text: 辰弥は笑ましげに頭をふり、さあ、私の申すのもすなわちここですて、なるほどあなたの御了簡では、書面進達さえ急に運べば、万事は後日のこととして、差しつかえはないとおっしゃるのも御もっともではあるが、その願書のことについては、私一人ではどうあっても計らいかぬる場合と申すは、かねてお話しもしてある通り、一体国友商会のは、初手は私の担当であったが、今では局長が引き受けて、万事表面上商会の世話をしている仲であって見れば、すでに明日か二三日うちに願書が出来て、商会からこれを本省へ差し出す日には、途中におって邪魔をする好分別がさらにないので、よっては事の未然に先立って、かの局長をわが手に引き入れ、うまく説き込んで遠方へ旅行させるよりほかはありませぬ。すでに局長が東京におらず、また旅先から商会の願書を遠く牽制して出させぬようにしているうちには、私の方便で、監督署長の、それあのさっき来た頬髯の濃い男、とにかくかの男を利用して、この局面の衝に立たせ、私はどちらへも手を出さずに、ひそかに綱を引きましょうが、それには、万一のあった時、われわれ三人の生涯はあなたの犠牲とならねばならず、それも成功の後ならばともかく、それ、御存じの待合事件の後を受けて、またまた、そんな行跡が社会へ暴露した日には、実はよくないことですからねえ。

chapter_summaries.0: Part One at Komatsu spa in autumn decline. Tatsuya, ministry secretary on sick leave, hears koto and singing in annex, questions maid, is shown best room for rank and beard. He sees fat laughing old man at railing, walks to Ogi lake bower, glimpses maiden on second floor and takes her for singer, then meets her full beauty in bath corridor. Old man is Miyoshi Zenpei with daughter Mitsuyo; bath talk makes them intimates; Tatsuya learns names and wealth and privately marks Mitsuyo as beautiful prey and Zenpei as not to be let escape.

hard_spots.why_hard: Long tide-like Meiji landscape sentences with kanbun colouring (堆藍前にあり凝黛後にあり, 煙波縹緲, 漁唱菱歌) and bird/plant names. Do not prune into efficient setting; luxuriance is the world Tatsuya exploits and the innocent cover for pursuit. Keep periodic rhythm without ennobling into Victorian purple.

Mitsuyo 真実に six times, Zenpei mocks back 嘘に six times. Must stay repetitive and childish, not varied for elegance. Later bargaining echoes with きっと/ようございます certainty over her — preserve echo, do not smooth.

Reception vessels named vessel by vessel: 銀穂屋付き手炉, 一閑釣瓶煙草盆, 探幽, 三夕三幅対, 宗甫花入, 蒔絵盆, 金溜塗重香合, 碪手青磁香炉, 七宝紫檀卓, 銀蒼鷹置物, 光琳金屏風. Social satire and circumstantial density at once. Needs identification plus material specificity; do not summarise away. Ruby/old names need glossing in margin.

願書, 払い下げ, 借区, 閣令, 官報, 周旋料, 割賦金, 謝金, 待合事件. Corruption is concrete sequence of applications, first-filing rule, travel alibis. Must remain precise and slightly airless; do not turn into vague bribery atmosphere. 待合事件 (assignation scandal) is prior disgrace raising stakes — annotate.
Tsunao printed once as 鋼雄 for 綱雄. Almost certainly press/transcription slip. Do not invent character difference; normalise in English to Tsunao and note for editor to check 1895 Taiyo text.

Tatsuya ore soliloquy (兵は神速, こん粉微塵) must sound exuberant/comic, not brooding; demand お貰い申しましたよ is brutal plain; close われはこの後のことを知らず with double rhetorical questions must not name wife or philosopher. English pronouns/connectives must keep knowing-and-not-knowing.

motifs.english: Keep same English word each time: 'beard' (with black/thick where source adds). Do not vary to whiskers/moustache. It marks fashionable manhood and trips the comedy when Mitsuyo insults Tsunao's beard and remembers Tatsuya's.
motifs.why: Admired splendid beard, accidental insult, returning official with thick side-whiskers. Deliberate echo of worldly masculinity.

motifs.english: Keep 'Hotei' with gloss once (squat laughing god), then repeat Hotei bulk/laugh. Keep 'laugh' verb repeated for Zenpei rather than varying to chuckle/guffaw.
motifs.why: Softens everything Zenpei does until it does not; warmth that makes treating daughter as asset possible.

motifs.english: Keep 'cigar smoke' / 'puffed smoke' language steady. Smoke pauses mark calculation admiring its own plan.
motifs.why: Appetite taking a pause. Punctuates Tatsuya scheming and Zenpei self-satisfaction; links pleasure to plotting.

motifs.english: Keep Mitsuyo's 'truly, truly, truly...' unvaried and excessive; keep Zenpei's mocking 'lies, lies...' parallel. Later keep bargaining 'certainly / without fail / promise' flat and repeated to let horror rhyme.
motifs.why: Childish insistence becomes contractual certainty. Do not elegant-vary; structure depends on echo.

motifs.english: Keep 'voice' and 'listen' wording: singing voice, listening ear, still listening. Do not resolve singer early; preserve inference.
motifs.motif: music behind the screen and listening
motifs.why: Mitsuyo first exists as sound; Tatsuya at lake still listening back to shoji. Governs desire as overhearing and pursuit as innocent aesthetic attention.

narration.english_tense: Past as default for narrative action; preserve scenic present participles only where Japanese scenic period invites sustained tableau, without flipping whole story into historic present. Dialogue past/present as spoken. Soliloquy in vivid present.
narration.frame: Third-person impersonal lyrical narrator with free access to private thought and soliloquy, but who withdraws at the end into professed ignorance. Linear seasonal movement autumn spa to autumn Tokyo with accelerated intrigue and rumoured aftermath.
narration.narrator: Elevated Meiji literary narrator, never judging villain directly; moral shown by juxtaposition of surface charm and private counting. Closes with われ (I) refusing knowledge.
narration.tense_habits: Classical-literary auxiliaries (なり, ぬ, たり, けり, ごとし) giving completed poetic past; scenery in sustained periodic present-like tableau; dialogue in Meiji colloquial -ます/-だ. Shifts freely without signalling interior vs exterior.
timeline: Autumn: Tatsuya convalescing at Komatsu Umeya inn meets singing, Zenpei and Mitsuyo; walks, bath familiarity, learns names and wealth (p2-p16).
Next day(s): Go games, Zenpei-Mitsuyo pillow comedy, walk with Mitsuyo, Tsunao arrival, quarrel, Tsunao silent departure (p19-p83).
Immediate return to Tokyo: Zenpei telegrams over Kijima mine tip, Mitsuyo waits for Tsunao, Tatsuya becomes household intimate and spider (p85-p96).
Banquet and private bargain: commission/annual thanks-money, riddle of Mitsuyo, cabinet-order draft for first-filing win and demand of Mitsuyo (p97-p130).
Aftermath withheld: rumour of Tatsuya wife and philosopher recluse, seasonal close (p132).

part_summaries.summary: Part One at Komatsu spa in autumn decline. Tatsuya, ministry secretary on sick leave, hears koto and singing in annex, questions maid, is shown best room for rank and beard. He sees fat laughing old man at railing, walks to Ogi lake bower, glimpses maiden on second floor and takes her for singer, then meets her full beauty in bath corridor. Old man is Miyoshi Zenpei with daughter Mitsuyo; bath talk makes them intimates; Tatsuya learns names and wealth and privately marks Mitsuyo as beautiful prey and Zenpei as not to be let escape.

Part Two in Zenpei rooms. After half-day go, Zenpei praises Tatsuya rank and talent and disparages Tsunao; Mitsuyo defends Tsunao as younger, refined, calm, high-spirited. Teasing about Tsunao visit turns into father-daughter pillow comedy with six-times truly tantrum, threats to break incense box and spoil haori, seized air-pillow. Zenpei offers tea, Mitsuyo goes to bath. Establishes indulgence as household language and Tsunao as expected ally.

Part Three morning walk to lake shore. Tatsuya presses Mitsuyo to walk, shifts through light talk and confesses listening to her koto; she deflects to scenery. Lush lake tableau. On return they meet Zenpei bringing stranger Tojo Tsunao; Mitsuyo runs alive to him, mocks his beard then catches Tatsuya black beard and laughs apology. Introductions chill: Tsunao arrogant, Tatsuya inwardly hostile; Zenpei alone imagines mutual respect. Four walk back, Mitsuyo childishly runs ahead for souvenir.

Part Four split scene. Tatsuya alone in ore voice vows to crush Tojo to powder, take Mitsuyo at one blow, hook father to cover debts, speed is everything, summons Zenpei via maid. Intercut: Zenpei urges Tsunao to bend and associate; Tsunao refuses as floating thin man; Mitsuyo agrees she dislikes Tatsuya; Zenpei defends sociability; quarrel, Tatsuya summons arrives, Zenpei storms out, Mitsuyo begs Tsunao to bend and stay by her, Tsunao will not bend self, talks of leaving, tender wavering then refusal; country singing and masseur mark time. Tsunao leaves without farewell to either, leaving letter; car sound fades.

Part Five return. Zenpei returns calling for Tsunao, learns flight, forgets it for three telegrams on Kijima coal mine tip from Tatsuya: cheap at 200,000, worth 500,000, quality beyond Miike, naval contracts. Mitsuyo bored and uncomforted asks to go home; Zenpei plans hasty Tokyo return for arrangements. Corridor meeting with Tatsuya, Mitsuyo turns away; men whisper laugh; Tatsuya sends regards to Tsunao. Mine displaces daughter in attention.

Part Six in Tokyo autumn. Mitsuyo rushes to Tsunao who has not returned; Zenpei races east-west in consultations; Tatsuya becomes daily intimate, spider thread over whole house from maid to retiree while Mitsuyo alone grows hostile and waits gaunt for Tsunao. Great reception prepared vessel by vessel for Tatsuya and important guests; Mitsuyo pleads bellyache and hides weeping unvisited. After guests leave, private bargain: 10,000 handling plus 1,000 yearly thanks-money, shares to colleagues, blocking Kunitomo application via bureau chief travel and supervisor front, risk of exposure after machiai scandal; Zenpei agrees, Tatsuya presses promise of anything in his power and riddles at what Zenpei has made. Night payment hint 25,000 yen; Tatsuya stays at Shimbashi as usual.

Part Seven break and final trap. Tsunao return rumoured but does not visit; Zenpei resents contempt, mother counts scholar slights; Mitsuyo secretly visits absent Tsunao then finds he came in her absence. Zenpei in rage declares Mitsuyo-Tsunao understanding broken. Mining race intensifies to 350,000 yen estimates, cabinet ordinance to decide by conditions and first filing. Tatsuya lures Zenpei to secret assignation upstairs, reveals draft ordinance obtained, promises certain flag if paper filed instantly on publication, demands reward: Mitsuyo herself — O-morai moshimashita. Narrator withdraws: does not know aftermath; Tatsuya said to have taken wife — who?; someone cast trouble away for half-life philosophy — who?; autumn wind over Ogi and paulownia; whose turn tomorrow.

body.say: Charm must stay charming and procedure stay procedural; do not rescue Tsunao into heroism, do not judge Tatsuya early, do not resolve the withheld ending.

style_sheet.annotation_density: Moderate: gloss spa, rank/title, mine system, vessels and ordinance terms, assignation-house and Shimbashi usage, Hotei and Kōrin references. Never annotate what context supplies; never use note to moralise or resolve ending.
style_sheet.author_voice: Three movements: lush periodic scenery (long tide-like sentences, autumn plants, water, light) kept lush but readable; sharp colloquial dialogue where each speaker breaks register; flat concrete procedure for bribes and papers. Keep movement audible; do not flatten into uniform fluent novel prose. Avoid Berman tidying: no rationalised syntax, no clarified subjects, no ennobled diction, no varied synonyms for deliberate repeats.
style_sheet.honorifics_and_names: Japanese order surname-given (Miyoshi Zenpei, Okumura Tatsuya) with macrons (Tōjō Tsunao, Miyoshi Mitsuyo) on first use; thereafter surname or given as Japanese does. Keep -san / -sama / -sama vs -san difference in romanised suffix because rank-climbing and intimacy live in it; explain once. Keep Sensei only if text uses 先生 (it does not; do not import). Servant/master terms (旦那-like 亭主, お方様) rendered to show deference without Victorianism.
style_sheet.keep_in_japanese: Vessel and art terms with gloss once then English:探幽 (Tan'yū school painting), 仁清香合 (Ninsei incense box), 碪手青磁 (kinuta celadon), 光琳風 (Kōrin style). Keep realia: 梅屋 (Umeya), 停車場 spelling flavour, 待合 (assignation house), 官報 (Official Gazette), 閣令 (cabinet ordinance) with brief note. Keep cigar as 葉巻/シガー signal.
style_sheet.quotation: Japanese binds dialogue in narrative without consistent quotes; use English double quotes for direct speech, single for thought-as-utterance where needed. Keep unattributed turns unattributed where Japanese leaves speaker to infer; do not add tags to tidy.
style_sheet.register: Narrative high-literary but not archaic: plain strong English with periodic length for scenery. Dialogue colloquial Meiji Tokyo: Zenpei bluff and familiar, Mitsuyo girlish polite with prolongation and pout, Tsunao stiff formal, Tatsuya accommodating chameleon. Soliloquy coarse ore energy, comic and brisk, not Gothic.
style_sheet.ruby_and_italics: Use italics for Japanese retentions (-san/-sama, vessel names, realia) on first setting and sparingly after. Render ruby glosses (笆まがき, 媚こぶる etc.) only where reading changes sense; otherwise silent. Do not italicise repeated motif English words.

english: The dew beneath the wild bush-clover that woos the wicker fence already held the colour of autumn. People vied with one another to hasten home. Upstairs and downstairs of the Umeya, which holds the first place for fine scenery among the hot springs of Komatsu and had been so thronged and merry, now, drawn to sadness by the deer-cries that reached across the ridge, the tread of feet passing to and fro along the corridors grew faintly lonely. Rickshaw after rickshaw, most of them laden with travelling bags and travellers, sped toward the station a ri away. The maids, grown long familiar and fond through the coming and going of trays and of tea, watched the receding figures go and stood a while lingering. The valley stream that winds before the house flowed far away with a murmuring rush. Was it a thrush that sang in the forest beyond?

The mountain fastness that once had known no means for its morning and evening livelihood has gained, with the summer visitors year by year, an unlooked-for increase of smoke, and tiled roofs show here and there through the leaves. Clouds lay along the ridge, rising from the roots of a pine of surpassing height to trail above the ivy that clings to the crags. Ranges standing on and on hide the sky of the market town, and the thousand streaks of waterfalls tumbling in rivalry toss abroad as it were threads of silver. To the north, as far as the eye can reach the gaze is far, the deer-fences stand stark and the clappers run far in a line, and the autumn of the mountain paddies looks busy. To the west the water shows its far destination, fold on fold of mountains, fold on fold of cloud, birds fly high and the leaves turn of themselves. One or two grass-cutting children, rich at heart, walk their horses slowly and sing after one another in blithe tunes, even now climbing the skirts of the outer hills.

The waves of Lake Ogi were very still. Faintly to be seen were leaf-boats, coaxed by the storm, slipping to hide behind the islands. Just then, brushing aside the wind in the pines, the exquisite sound of a koto rose from a room on the second floor. The newly arrived guest in the detached pavilion inclined his ear.
takes.label: Polished surface, predatory undertow
takes.line: Recommended first take. Narration should be supple and handsome enough to make the inn, the lake and Tatsuya himself pleasurable, with long scenic sentences allowed to gather before they break. Tatsuya speaks with easy masculine confidence and adapts instantly; alone he is quicker, blunter and more delighted, but never melodramatic. Zenpei is expansive, wheezing, pleased with himself. Mitsuyo is bright, spoiled, rapid and intimate, not quaint. Tsunao is clipped, elevated and awkward, his correctness costing him warmth. Wrong for this take: slangy modernisation, Victorian pastiche, or a narratorial sneer that tells the reader Tatsuya is false before his actions do.

english: The dew under the wild bush clover that fondles the wattle fence had already the color of autumn. People vied to hurry home. Upstairs and down, the Umeya, which holds first place for beauty among the baths of Komatsu and had been all bustle, now, moved to sadness by the stags calling across the ridge, let its footsteps passing in the corridors grow a little forlorn. Rickshaw after rickshaw, most of them laden with traveling bags and guests, ran for the station a ri ahead. The maids, grown close and familiar through long carrying of trays and tea, watched the departing backs a while and stood lingering. The mountain stream that rings the front flowed murmuring far away. Was it a thrush singing in the forest beyond.

The mountain depths, which had known no smoke morning or evening, had gained unlooked for smoke with the summer guests year by year, and tiled roofs showed here and there through the leaves. There were clouds above the ridge, rising from the roots of one surpassingly tall pine to trail over the ivy that clings to the rocks. The unbroken peaks hid the sky of the market town, and the thousand streaks of competing falls shook out like tangled threads of silver. To the north, as far as the eye reaches, the deer fences stand stark and the clappers run far in a line, and the autumn of the mountain paddies looks busy. To the west the water shows its far course, mountains upon mountains, clouds upon clouds, birds flying high and leaves turning of themselves. One or two grass cutting children, rich at heart, walking their horses along and singing a merry tune together, were just now climbing the skirts of the outer hill.

The waves of Lake Ogi were very still. Leaf boats coaxed by the storm showed faintly where their shadows slipped behind the islands. Just then, brushing the wind from the pines, the exquisite sound of a koto rose from a room on the second floor. The newly come guest in the detached room inclined his ear.
takes.label: Drier social satire
takes.line: Narration plainer and more ironic, the scenic passages kept but tightened, the comedy of rank, antiques and fees allowed to sound almost dry. Tatsuya becomes a superior operator among operators; Zenpei funnier and more nakedly acquisitive; Tsunao’s stiffness more obviously a social defect. This gains speed and bite, but risks losing the genuine sensuous attraction of the hot-spring world and turning Mitsuyo’s danger into an epigram. Wrong for it: contemporary bureaucratic jargon or satire so broad that Zenpei ceases to be a doting father.

english: The wild bush-clover fawning upon the wattle fence, the dew beneath it already wears the colour of autumn. People vie with one another to hasten home. Upstairs and down, the Umeya, which holds the first place for beauty among the hot springs of Komatsu and was lately so thronged with merry company, now, moved to sorrow by the deer-whistles sounding across the ridge, hears the footsteps passing in its corridors grown somewhat lonely. Carriage after carriage, most of them laden with travelling bags and guests, runs toward the station a ri ahead. The maids, long grown familiar and close through the carrying of trays and the carrying of tea, stand a while even so to watch the departing figures away. The mountain stream circling before it flows on afar with a murmuring rush. Is it a thrush that sings in the forest yonder?

Even in these mountains, where morning and evening sustenance was once unknown, the summer guests of each year have added unlooked-for smoke, and tiled roofs show here and there through the leaves. There is cloud upon the ridge, rising from the roots of one towering pine to trail over the ivy tangled upon the rocks. The serried peaks hide the sky of the market town, and the thousand streaks of falling cataracts toss about like tangled threads of silver. To the north, as far as the eye can reach, the deer-fences stand stark and the clappers run far in line, and the autumn in the mountain paddies looks busy. To the west the water shows its far destination, mountains upon mountains and clouds upon clouds, birds fly high and the leaves turn of themselves. One or two grass-cutting children, rich at heart, walking their horses and singing a merry tune in turn, are now climbing the skirts of the outer mountain.

The waves of Lake Ogi are utterly still. The shadow of a leaf-boat coaxed by storm, slipping behind an island, faintly shows. Just then, brushing aside the wind in the pines, the exquisite sound of a koto rose from a room on the second floor. The newly come guest of the detached parlour bent his ear to listen.
takes.label: Fuller Meiji melodrama
takes.line: Narration more formal and emotionally open, with the lake, music and first sight of Mitsuyo given romantic amplitude. Tatsuya is smoother and more dangerous, Tsunao more evidently the honourable lover, Mitsuyo more lyrical and imperilled. This is playable and may suit serial publication, but it is the riskiest take: it can settle ambiguities the story withholds and make Tatsuya’s late demand feel like a villain’s unmasking rather than the logical price of everything before it. Wrong for it: fainting innocence, Byronic darkness, or consolation at the close.

options.author: first read (Wonder)
options.case: This is a study in social plausibility: Tatsuya wins not despite being charming but because charm, rank, flattery and appetite are indistinguishable in the world he moves through. The horror is that his predation has no special register. It sounds like energy, competence, even good humour, until the reader hears what it is counting. He ingratiates himself with the inn maids, Zenpei, Mitsuyo’s whole household, and finally with officials, while privately treating a government coal-mine disposal as plunder and Mitsuyo as part of the payment. Zenpei is not simply deceived: his vanity and greed make him enjoy being deceived. Tsunao sees Tatsuya at once, but rectitude without social grace looks pale, pedantic and ungenerous beside him. For the English: Keep the story’s surface genuinely charming. Tatsuya must work in English as he works in a room—quick, amusing, at ease—and then, alone, reveal himself in the same untroubled voice: Mitsuyo is “beautiful prey,” her father is to be hooked, his debts and the mining concession are parts of one campaign. Do not signal villainy in advance, do not make the soliloquy brooding or conscience-stricken, and do not soften its sporting delight. The shock depends on how little his tone changes.
options.tradeoff: Makes the exposure a matter of content overheard in an unchanged, socially plausible voice, so charm itself becomes the horror.

options.author: crux check (Wonder)
options.case:
The story is told in a high, lyrical, scenic narration that never lowers itself to judge its villain, while the moral exposure happens entirely through a split in Tatsuya's voice. The hot-spring landscape, lake, and seasonal close are rendered in ornate, impersonal periods (p2-p4, p37, p40), and the same surface covers a corrupt mining concession. Tatsuya is all polished deference with Zenpei and hosts (p7, p101-p112), but alone he becomes 'ore': Mitsuyo is a 'beautiful prize' (美しき獲物, p16), Tsunao is to be crushed 'konagona' (p48), and the mine, the father, and the girl are one rapid campaign — '兵は神速' (p49). Mitsuyo, by contrast, is characterised by unvaried insistence and repetition — 真実に six times in one outburst (p27) — which Zenpei then mocks by repetition back. Flatten any of this into uniformly fluent, psychologically explanatory English and Tatsuya becomes either a declared cad or a romantic suitor, and Mitsuyo a merely charming ingenue, instead of the predator and the child the juxtaposition shows. For the English: Keep a distinctly elevated, periodic narrative prose, but let dialogue break register sharply: Mitsuyo's repetitions and girl's protests must stay repetitive rather than be varied for elegance, Zenpei's bluff familiarity stay bluff, and Tatsuya must sound ingratiating in company and coarsely proprietorial alone. Do not make Tatsuya slangy throughout, or Mitsuyo more articulate and knowing than she is.
- The ending, and the narration throughout, withholds the very facts a reader most wants — who got Mitsuyo, what the bribery came to, who was punished — and that withholding is the story's verdict. Tatsuya's demand is made brutally explicit — the reward for the draft cabinet order is Mitsuyo herself: 'お貰い申しましたよ' (p130) — and then the narrator simply stops: 'われはこの後のことを知らず' (p132). What follows is only rumour and rhetorical question: Tatsuya has taken a wife, 'その妻は誰なるらん'; someone has thrown himself into philosophy, 'その人は誰なるらん'; '明日は誰が身の'. Earlier the same reticence governs motive and perception (the singer identified only by inference, p10; Tsunao and Tatsuya each privately misreading the other while Zenpei alone imagines mutual respect, p44). For the English: Preserve every refusal to resolve: do not name the wife, do not identify the philosopher beyond what the syntax leaves open, do not add a concluding moral, a marriage, a ruin, or an ironic wink that settles it. English pronouns and connectives must be chosen to keep the same degree of knowing-and-not-knowing as the Japanese.
options.tradeoff: Makes the exposure a marked split of register against elevated narration, and adds the narrator's withholding of outcome as a second, governing crux.

second.say:
## Crux check — second reader

**1. A beautiful narration that refuses to condemn, set against a villain who condemns himself only in private register.**

*Reason:* The hot-spring landscape, lake, and seasonal close are rendered in ornate, impersonal periods (p2–p4, p37, p40), and the same elevated surface covers a corrupt mining concession. Tatsuya is polished deference with Zenpei and the household (p7, p101–p112), but alone he is *ore*: Mitsuyo is a “beautiful prize” (美しき獲物, p16), Tsunao is to be crushed to powder (p48), and mine, father, and girl form one rapid campaign — “兵は神速” (p49). Mitsuyo is characterised by the opposite limitation: unvaried insistence, 真実に repeated six times in a single outburst (p27), which her father mocks by repeating it back.

*For the English:* Keep a distinctly elevated, periodic narrative prose, but let the voices break register sharply. Do not vary Mitsuyo’s repetitions for elegance, make her more knowing than she is, or make Tatsuya coarse throughout. His charm must remain plausible, because the exposure depends on hearing the private voice underneath it.

**2. An ending — and a narration — that withholds the facts on which any moral settlement would depend.**

*Reason:* Tatsuya’s demand is brutally explicit: his reward for the draft cabinet order is Mitsuyo herself, “お貰い申しましたよ” (p130). The narrator then stops: “われはこの後のことを知らず” (p132). There follows only rumour — Tatsuya has taken a wife, “その妻は誰なるらん”; someone has buried himself in philosophy, “その人は誰なるらん”; “明日は誰が身の”. The same reticence has governed perception throughout, from the singer identified only by inference (p10) to Tatsuya and Tsunao privately despising each other while Zenpei alone imagines mutual respect (p44).

*For the English:* Do not name the wife, identify the philosopher beyond what the syntax leaves open, or add a moral, marriage, ruin, or settling ironic wink. The English must preserve exactly this degree of knowing and not-knowing.

**Confidence:** High on both points; the register split and the final disclaimer are structural, not local effects. I would revise the first only if a fuller textual history showed the scenic narration to be conventional padding Bizan himself treated as disposable — nothing in this text suggests that.

open_questions.question: How formal is the understanding between Mitsuyo and Tsunao? The text calls him a relative, has Zenpei speak of an existing promise and then announce the match broken, and gives the young people unmistakable intimacy, but it never cleanly labels him fiancé. Should English preserve that social legibility without naming it more definitely than the Japanese does?
open_questions.why_it_matters: If they are made merely cousins, Tatsuya’s demand loses force; if they are made explicitly engaged too early, the father-daughter teasing and Mitsuyo’s behaviour become narrower and less ambiguous.

open_questions.question: How far does Mitsuyo understand what she dislikes in Tatsuya? Her distaste is instinctive and bodily—he is ‘creepy,’ ‘strange’—rather than analytical. How much adult perception should the English allow into that intuition without making her either knowingly prophetic or merely petulant?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Her limited understanding is the point at which the comedy turns uneasy. Too much clarity makes her a judge of the plot; too little makes her father’s disposal of her seem weightless.

open_questions.question: At the close, is the narrator’s ignorance a genuine refusal of knowledge, a teasing invitation to infer, or both? Tatsuya has taken a wife; someone has thrown worldly trouble away for philosophy. The parallels invite identification of wife and philosopher without confirming either.
open_questions.why_it_matters: The last paragraph must not be resolved by tone. A knowing wink would say Tatsuya got Mitsuyo; a melancholy certainty would canonise Tsunao. The Japanese leaves marriage, ruin, renunciation and success suspended together.

open_questions.question: How much of Zenpei’s antiquarian display and of the mining intrigue is deliberate social satire, and how much is straight Meiji circumstantiality? The named vessels, screens, bribes, intermediaries, ordinance and first-filed application give corruption a material density that a brisk English summary would lose.
open_questions.why_it_matters: Cutting or clarifying these passages would make the plot cleaner but remove the world that makes it possible: status objects, cash, procedure and access are the real love-language between Zenpei and Tatsuya.

open_questions.question: The source twice gives Tsunao’s name with a different first character. Is that a printing or transcription accident to be silently normalised in a reading, or a point that needs editorial checking against the 1895 text?
open_questions.why_it_matters: No interpretive weight should be built on it until the witness is checked; the English should be consistent, but the edition should not invent a variant reading.

body.reading:
The crux is that this story’s surface genuinely charms. Okumura Tatsuya, a ministry secretary convalescing at a hot-spring inn, wins not despite being plausible but because plausibility is his instrument. He is quick with maids, landlords, an ageing rich man, officials and strangers; he knows what each person wishes to hear. Alone, in the same brisk and untroubled voice, he counts Mitsuyo as “beautiful prey,” her father as a man not to be let escape, and the disposal of the Kijima mine as a field for fees, bribes and leverage. Do not let English darken him in advance. He must first be good company. Nor should his private monologue become Gothic villainy: it is exuberant, comic, almost boyish in its appetite—“my trick,” “let’s begin,” speed is everything. The chill comes because nothing in his manner admits a conflict.

Almost everyone is taken in, and the text is precise about why. Zenpei, fat, laughing, Hotei-like, is not a passive fool. He loves the sound of Tatsuya’s rank, loves being recognised as a man of consequence, and wants the mine to repair earlier losses. Flattery gives his greed a respectable social form. When he agrees to pay and then, drunk on success, promises Tatsuya anything within his power, his earlier riddle has already shown where the bargain can go. English must let Zenpei be warm and ridiculous without making him harmless: the same doting father who submits to Mitsuyo’s pillow-fight can treat her, an hour later, as an asset whose transfer requires only timing.

Against Tatsuya stands Tojo Tsunao, a new philosophy graduate, and the translation stands or falls on refusing to rescue him into conventional heroism. Tsunao is right about Tatsuya immediately and almost completely. He is also pale, stiff, censorious and socially hopeless; he cannot make a necessary concession, cannot laugh off an insult, and can only leave. Seen through the inn’s eyes, and often through the narration’s, he looks like exactly what Tatsuya calls him: a pedant who will bury his life in empty theory. Yet his rigidity is the only form integrity takes here. If English gives him warm authority, the contest becomes melodrama. If it makes him merely absurd, Tatsuya has won the prose as he wins every room. He must hold his ground and make the reader pay for seeing that he is right.

Mitsuyo is the third term, and not a prize with a face. She first exists for Tatsuya as music behind a shoji, then as a glimpse, then, after the bath, as an almost embarrassingly lingering inventory of beauty. But once she speaks she becomes specific: spoiled, theatrical, quick, physically affectionate with her father, intoxicated by Tsunao’s arrival and childishly triumphant that her ally has come. Her repeated “truly, truly, truly” when she claims to be angry, her threats to break the incense box and spoil her father’s haori, her seizure of the air-pillow, are not decorative maidenliness. They establish a household in which indulgence is a language—and therefore a girl who can be bargained away in that same language. She is drawn to Tsunao naturally, without coy uncertainty; she also dislikes Tatsuya before she can say why, finding him uncanny rather than merely disagreeable. Keep both. Do not make her a knowing moral judge, and do not make her ignorant in a way that cancels her intuition.

The sound of the piece moves between three kinds of writing, and flattening that movement would be a major loss. The openings and transitions are lush Meiji scene-painting: long, tide-like sentences crowded with autumn bush-clover, lake water, waterfalls, inn corridors, thrushes and distant clappers. These passages should not be pruned into efficient setting. Their luxuriance is the world Tatsuya knows how to enjoy and exploit, and the lake-shore walk matters because beauty keeps offering an innocent explanation for his pursuit. Against this set the dialogue: Zenpei bluff and self-delighted, Mitsuyo bright with feminine Tokyo colloquialism and wheedling repetition, Tsunao formal to the point of bruising himself, Tatsuya shifting register for every listener. The third kind is procedure: ministry, bureau chief, supervisor, applications, a cabinet ordinance, first submission, commissions and annual “thanks-money.” It should remain concrete and slightly airless. Corruption here is not atmosphere. It is a sequence of doors, intermediaries and papers.

Certain repetitions carry structure. Tatsuya’s black beard is admired, joked about, accidentally insulted by Mitsuyo when she attacks Tsunao’s beard, and returns as a social sign of the fashionable man of the world. Zenpei’s laughter and Hotei bulk soften everything he does until they do not. Smoke from Tatsuya’s cigar punctuates moments of calculation, as if appetite itself were taking a pause to admire its plan. Mitsuyo’s “truly” in her tantrum is later answered, horribly, by the bargaining dialogue in which men say “certainly” and “without fail” over her. Preserve the echoes where they occur. Do not vary repeated phrases simply because English prose is taught to.

The most likely fluent failure is to tidy the intrigue into a clear contest between seducer and fiancé, with explanatory transitions and a decisive emotional climax. The Japanese instead lets domestic comedy take up room, lets a reception be described vessel by vessel, lets Tsunao walk out without farewells, and then accelerates. Zenpei returns from Tatsuya not even seeing his daughter’s tears because the mine has entered his head. That displacement—people looking straight past one another toward the desired object—is the story’s governing action. Look for it everywhere: Tatsuya at the lake still listening for a voice behind the shoji; Zenpei hearing rank rather than character; the family welcoming Tatsuya while Mitsuyo alone grows more hostile; mother and father counting Tsunao’s social failures when his moral perception has become inconvenient.

The ending must be left exactly as unresolved as the narrator leaves it. After Tatsuya asks for Mitsuyo as his “reward,” the text withdraws. It does not show acceptance, refusal, marriage, ruin or rescue. The narrator says he does not know what followed: Tatsuya is said to have taken a wife—who is she? Someone has cast off worldly trouble to devote a half-life to philosophy—who is he? Do not let word choice answer. The questions are inviting and desolate at once, and the final seasonal glance does not console. The most dangerous English additions would be a hint that virtue has been rewarded, that Tatsuya has been punished, or that Mitsuyo has understood her fate. None of that is given. What is given is a world so well arranged for Tatsuya that the reader must supply, and therefore fear, the likely result.

voice_takes.label: Polished surface, predatory undertow
voice_takes.line: Recommended first take. Narration should be supple and handsome enough to make the inn, the lake and Tatsuya himself pleasurable, with long scenic sentences allowed to gather before they break. Tatsuya speaks with easy masculine confidence and adapts instantly; alone he is quicker, blunter and more delighted, but never melodramatic. Zenpei is expansive, wheezing, pleased with himself. Mitsuyo is bright, spoiled, rapid and intimate, not quaint. Tsunao is clipped, elevated and awkward, his correctness costing him warmth. Wrong for this take: slangy modernisation, Victorian pastiche, or a narratorial sneer that tells the reader Tatsuya is false before his actions do.
