fork.question: Do the readers name the same crux in different words, or different cruxes — in particular, does Tatsuya's predation speak in the same untroubled voice as his charm, or in a coarsely proprietorial voice split from it, and is the ending's refusal to resolve part of the crux or not?

options.author: first-read (Wonder)
options.case: - This is a study in social plausibility: Tatsuya wins not despite being charming but because charm, rank, flattery and appetite are indistinguishable in the world he moves through. The horror is that his predation has no special register. It sounds like energy, competence, even good humour, until the reader hears what it is counting. He ingratiates himself with the inn maids, Zenpei, Mitsuyo’s whole household, and finally with officials, while privately treating a government coal-mine disposal as plunder and Mitsuyo as part of the payment. Zenpei is not simply deceived: his vanity and greed make him enjoy being deceived. Tsunao sees Tatsuya at once, but rectitude without social grace looks pale, pedantic and ungenerous beside him. For the English: Keep the story’s surface genuinely charming. Tatsuya must work in English as he works in a room—quick, amusing, at ease—and then, alone, reveal himself in the same untroubled voice: Mitsuyo is “beautiful prey,” her father is to be hooked, his debts and the mining concession are parts of one campaign. Do not signal villainy in advance, do not make the soliloquy brooding or conscience-stricken, and do not soften its sporting delight. The shock depends on how little his tone changes.
options.tradeoff: Makes the exposure a matter of content overheard in an unchanged, socially plausible voice, so charm itself becomes the horror.

options.author: crux-check (Wonder)
options.case:
- The story is told in a high, lyrical, scenic narration that never lowers itself to judge its villain, while the moral exposure happens entirely through a split in Tatsuya's voice. The hot-spring landscape, lake, and seasonal close are rendered in ornate, impersonal periods (p2-p4, p37, p40), and the same surface covers a corrupt mining concession. Tatsuya is all polished deference with Zenpei and hosts (p7, p101-p112), but alone he becomes 'ore': Mitsuyo is a 'beautiful prize' (美しき獲物, p16), Tsunao is to be crushed 'konagona' (p48), and the mine, the father, and the girl are one rapid campaign — '兵は神速' (p49). Mitsuyo, by contrast, is characterised by unvaried insistence and repetition — 真実に six times in one outburst (p27) — which Zenpei then mocks by repetition back. Flatten any of this into uniformly fluent, psychologically explanatory English and Tatsuya becomes either a declared cad or a romantic suitor, and Mitsuyo a merely charming ingenue, instead of the predator and the child the juxtaposition shows. For the English: Keep a distinctly elevated, periodic narrative prose, but let dialogue break register sharply: Mitsuyo's repetitions and girl's protests must stay repetitive rather than be varied for elegance, Zenpei's bluff familiarity stay bluff, and Tatsuya must sound ingratiating in company and coarsely proprietorial alone. Do not make Tatsuya slangy throughout, or Mitsuyo more articulate and knowing than she is.
- The ending, and the narration throughout, withholds the very facts a reader most wants — who got Mitsuyo, what the bribery came to, who was punished — and that withholding is the story's verdict. Tatsuya's demand is made brutally explicit — the reward for the draft cabinet order is Mitsuyo herself: 'お貰い申しましたよ' (p130) — and then the narrator simply stops: 'われはこの後のことを知らず' (p132). What follows is only rumour and rhetorical question: Tatsuya has taken a wife, 'その妻は誰なるらん'; someone has thrown himself into philosophy, 'その人は誰なるらん'; '明日は誰が身の'. Earlier the same reticence governs motive and perception (the singer identified only by inference, p10; Tsunao and Tatsuya each privately misreading the other while Zenpei alone imagines mutual respect, p44). For the English: Preserve every refusal to resolve: do not name the wife, do not identify the philosopher beyond what the syntax leaves open, do not add a concluding moral, a marriage, a ruin, or an ironic wink that settles it. English pronouns and connectives must be chosen to keep the same degree of knowing-and-not-knowing as the Japanese.
options.tradeoff: Makes the exposure a marked split of register against elevated narration, and adds the narrator's withholding of outcome as a second, governing crux.

fork.head_reason: They do not name the same thing in different words. They agree that Tatsuya's charm carries his predation, but they contradict each other on the mechanism that a translation must reproduce: Option 0 stakes everything on how little his tone changes alone, while Option 1 stakes it on a sharp register split — polished deference in company, 'ore' and 'konagona' alone — set against elevated narration, and adds a second crux Option 0 never mentions, the narration's withholding of outcome. That difference will govern Tatsuya's voice on every page and the handling of the close, so being wrong would be expensive and the text as presented does not settle it for the desk.

## Crux check — second reader

**1. A beautiful narration that refuses to condemn, set against a villain who condemns himself only in private register.**

*Reason:* The hot-spring landscape, lake, and seasonal close are rendered in ornate, impersonal periods (p2–p4, p37, p40), and the same elevated surface covers a corrupt mining concession. Tatsuya is polished deference with Zenpei and the household (p7, p101–p112), but alone he is *ore*: Mitsuyo is a “beautiful prize” (美しき獲物, p16), Tsunao is to be crushed to powder (p48), and mine, father, and girl form one rapid campaign — “兵は神速” (p49). Mitsuyo is characterised by the opposite limitation: unvaried insistence, 真実に repeated six times in a single outburst (p27), which her father mocks by repeating it back.

*For the English:* Keep a distinctly elevated, periodic narrative prose, but let the voices break register sharply. Do not vary Mitsuyo’s repetitions for elegance, make her more knowing than she is, or make Tatsuya coarse throughout. His charm must remain plausible, because the exposure depends on hearing the private voice underneath it.

**2. An ending — and a narration — that withholds the facts on which any moral settlement would depend.**

*Reason:* Tatsuya’s demand is brutally explicit: his reward for the draft cabinet order is Mitsuyo herself, “お貰い申しましたよ” (p130). The narrator then stops: “われはこの後のことを知らず” (p132). There follows only rumour — Tatsuya has taken a wife, “その妻は誰なるらん”; someone has buried himself in philosophy, “その人は誰なるらん”; “明日は誰が身の”. The same reticence has governed perception throughout, from the singer identified only by inference (p10) to Tatsuya and Tsunao privately despising each other while Zenpei alone imagines mutual respect (p44).

*For the English:* Do not name the wife, identify the philosopher beyond what the syntax leaves open, or add a moral, marriage, ruin, or settling ironic wink. The English must preserve exactly this degree of knowing and not-knowing.

**Confidence:** High on both points; the register split and the final disclaimer are structural, not local effects. I would revise the first only if a fuller textual history showed the scenic narration to be conventional padding Bizan himself treated as disposable — nothing in this text suggests that.

The readers name overlapping material but different cruxes: Option 0 locates the horror in Tatsuya's unchanged voice, Option 1 in a register split plus withheld resolution, and those give opposite instructions for the English. I am opening a fork rather than merging them. Recommendation: proceed on Option 1 until you rule, because it alone ties its claim to checkable features of the text — the 'ore' soliloquy, the repetitions, 'われはこの後のことを知らず' — whereas Option 0's 'same untroubled voice' would have to override that pronoun and register evidence; but if you judge the split to be a matter of situation rather than of voice, Option 0's reading of social plausibility is the one to adopt whole. The hot-spring landscape, lake, and seasonal close are rendered in ornate, impersonal periods (p2-p4, p37, p40), and the same surface covers a corrupt mining concession. Tatsuya is all polished deference with Zenpei and hosts (p7, p101-p112), but alone he becomes 'ore': Mitsuyo is a 'beautiful prize' (美しき獲物, p16), Tsunao is to be crushed 'konagona' (p48), and the mine, the father, and the girl are one rapid campaign — '兵は神速' (p49). Mitsuyo, by contrast, is characterised by unvaried insistence and repetition — 真実に six times in one outburst (p27) — which Zenpei then mocks by repetition back. Flatten any of this into uniformly fluent, psychologically explanatory English and Tatsuya becomes either a declared cad or a romantic suitor, and Mitsuyo a merely charming ingenue, instead of the predator and the child the juxtaposition shows. For the English: Keep a distinctly elevated, periodic narrative prose, but let dialogue break register sharply: Mitsuyo's repetitions and girl's protests must stay repetitive rather than be varied for elegance, Zenpei's bluff familiarity stay bluff, and Tatsuya must sound ingratiating in company and coarsely proprietorial alone. Do not make Tatsuya slangy throughout, or Mitsuyo more articulate and knowing than she is.
- The ending, and the narration throughout, withholds the very facts a reader most wants — who got Mitsuyo, what the bribery came to, who was punished — and that withholding is the story's verdict. Tatsuya's demand is made brutally explicit — the reward for the draft cabinet order is Mitsuyo herself: 'お貰い申しましたよ' (p130) — and then the narrator simply stops: 'われはこの後のことを知らず' (p132). What follows is only rumour and rhetorical question: Tatsuya has taken a wife, 'その妻は誰なるらん'; someone has thrown himself into philosophy, 'その人は誰なるらん'; '明日は誰が身の'. Earlier the same reticence governs motive and perception (the singer identified only by inference, p10; Tsunao and Tatsuya each privately misreading the other while Zenpei alone imagines mutual respect, p44). For the English: Preserve every refusal to resolve: do not name the wife, do not identify the philosopher beyond what the syntax leaves open, do not add a concluding moral, a marriage, a ruin, or an ironic wink that settles it. English pronouns and connectives must be chosen to keep the same degree of knowing-and-not-knowing as the Japanese.
options.tradeoff: Makes the exposure a marked split of register against elevated narration, and adds the narrator's withholding of outcome as a second, governing crux.

second.say:
## Crux check — second reader

**1. A beautiful narration that refuses to condemn, set against a villain who condemns himself only in private register.**

*Reason:* The hot-spring landscape, lake, and seasonal close are rendered in ornate, impersonal periods (p2–p4, p37, p40), and the same elevated surface covers a corrupt mining concession. Tatsuya is polished deference with Zenpei and the household (p7, p101–p112), but alone he is *ore*: Mitsuyo is a “beautiful prize” (美しき獲物, p16), Tsunao is to be crushed to powder (p48), and mine, father, and girl form one rapid campaign — “兵は神速” (p49). Mitsuyo is characterised by the opposite limitation: unvaried insistence, 真実に repeated six times in a single outburst (p27), which her father mocks by repeating it back.

*For the English:* Keep a distinctly elevated, periodic narrative prose, but let the voices break register sharply. Do not vary Mitsuyo’s repetitions for elegance, make her more knowing than she is, or make Tatsuya coarse throughout. His charm must remain plausible, because the exposure depends on hearing the private voice underneath it.

**2. An ending — and a narration — that withholds the facts on which any moral settlement would depend.**

*Reason:* Tatsuya’s demand is brutally explicit: his reward for the draft cabinet order is Mitsuyo herself, “お貰い申しましたよ” (p130). The narrator then stops: “われはこの後のことを知らず” (p132). There follows only rumour — Tatsuya has taken a wife, “その妻は誰なるらん”; someone has buried himself in philosophy, “その人は誰なるらん”; “明日は誰が身の”. The same reticence has governed perception throughout, from the singer identified only by inference (p10) to Tatsuya and Tsunao privately despising each other while Zenpei alone imagines mutual respect (p44).

*For the English:* Do not name the wife, identify the philosopher beyond what the syntax leaves open, or add a moral, marriage, ruin, or settling ironic wink. The English must preserve exactly this degree of knowing and not-knowing.

**Confidence:** High on both points; the register split and the final disclaimer are structural, not local effects. I would revise the first only if a fuller textual history showed the scenic narration to be conventional padding Bizan himself treated as disposable — nothing in this text suggests that.
second.what_would_change_my_mind: Evidence from a fuller textual history that the scenic narration was conventional padding Bizan treated as disposable; nothing in this text suggests that.

crux.for_the_english: Keep the story’s surface genuinely charming. Tatsuya must work in English as he works in a room—quick, amusing, at ease—and then, alone, reveal himself in the same untroubled voice: Mitsuyo is “beautiful prey,” her father is to be hooked, his debts and the mining concession are parts of one campaign. Do not signal villainy in advance, do not make the soliloquy brooding or conscience-stricken, and do not soften its sporting delight. The shock depends on how little his tone changes.
crux.point: This is a study in social plausibility: Tatsuya wins not despite being charming but because charm, rank, flattery and appetite are indistinguishable in the world he moves through. The horror is that his predation has no special register. It sounds like energy, competence, even good humour, until the reader hears what it is counting.
crux.why: He ingratiates himself with the inn maids, Zenpei, Mitsuyo’s whole household, and finally with officials, while privately treating a government coal-mine disposal as plunder and Mitsuyo as part of the payment. Zenpei is not simply deceived: his vanity and greed make him enjoy being deceived. Tsunao sees Tatsuya at once, but rectitude without social grace looks pale, pedantic and ungenerous beside him.

Drafted the opening autumn tableau at Komatsu, keeping the scenic periods long.

english: The dew beneath the wild bush-clover that woos the wicker fence already held the colour of autumn. People vied with one another to hasten home. Upstairs and downstairs of the Umeya, which holds the first place for fine scenery among the hot springs of Komatsu and had been so thronged and merry, now, drawn to sadness by the deer-cries that reached across the ridge, the tread of feet passing to and fro along the corridors grew faintly lonely. Rickshaw after rickshaw, most of them laden with travelling bags and travellers, sped toward the station a ri away. The maids, grown long familiar and fond through the coming and going of trays and of tea, watched the receding figures go and stood a while lingering. The valley stream that winds before the house flowed far away with a murmuring rush. Was it a thrush that sang in the forest beyond?

The mountain fastness that once had known no means for its morning and evening livelihood has gained, with the summer visitors year by year, an unlooked-for increase of smoke, and tiled roofs show here and there through the leaves. Clouds lay along the ridge, rising from the roots of a pine of surpassing height to trail above the ivy that clings to the crags. Ranges standing on and on hide the sky of the market town, and the thousand streaks of waterfalls tumbling in rivalry toss abroad as it were threads of silver. To the north, as far as the eye can reach the gaze is far, the deer-fences stand stark and the clappers run far in a line, and the autumn of the mountain paddies looks busy. To the west the water shows its far destination, fold on fold of mountains, fold on fold of cloud, birds fly high and the leaves turn of themselves. One or two grass-cutting children, rich at heart, walk their horses slowly and sing after one another in blithe tunes, even now climbing the skirts of the outer hills.

The waves of Lake Ogi were very still. Faintly to be seen were leaf-boats, coaxed by the storm, slipping to hide behind the islands. Just then, brushing aside the wind in the pines, the exquisite sound of a koto rose from a room on the second floor. The newly arrived guest in the detached pavilion inclined his ear.
takes.label: Polished surface, predatory undertow
takes.line: Recommended first take. Narration should be supple and handsome enough to make the inn, the lake and Tatsuya himself pleasurable, with long scenic sentences allowed to gather before they break. Tatsuya speaks with easy masculine confidence and adapts instantly; alone he is quicker, blunter and more delighted, but never melodramatic. Zenpei is expansive, wheezing, pleased with himself. Mitsuyo is bright, spoiled, rapid and intimate, not quaint. Tsunao is clipped, elevated and awkward, his correctness costing him warmth. Wrong for this take: slangy modernisation, Victorian pastiche, or a narratorial sneer that tells the reader Tatsuya is false before his actions do.

english: The dew under the wild bush clover that fondles the wattle fence had already the color of autumn. People vied to hurry home. Upstairs and down, the Umeya, which holds first place for beauty among the baths of Komatsu and had been all bustle, now, moved to sadness by the stags calling across the ridge, let its footsteps passing in the corridors grow a little forlorn. Rickshaw after rickshaw, most of them laden with traveling bags and guests, ran for the station a ri ahead. The maids, grown close and familiar through long carrying of trays and tea, watched the departing backs a while and stood lingering. The mountain stream that rings the front flowed murmuring far away. Was it a thrush singing in the forest beyond.

The mountain depths, which had known no smoke morning or evening, had gained unlooked for smoke with the summer guests year by year, and tiled roofs showed here and there through the leaves. There were clouds above the ridge, rising from the roots of one surpassingly tall pine to trail over the ivy that clings to the rocks. The unbroken peaks hid the sky of the market town, and the thousand streaks of competing falls shook out like tangled threads of silver. To the north, as far as the eye reaches, the deer fences stand stark and the clappers run far in a line, and the autumn of the mountain paddies looks busy. To the west the water shows its far course, mountains upon mountains, clouds upon clouds, birds flying high and leaves turning of themselves. One or two grass cutting children, rich at heart, walking their horses along and singing a merry tune together, were just now climbing the skirts of the outer hill.

The waves of Lake Ogi were very still. Leaf boats coaxed by the storm showed faintly where their shadows slipped behind the islands. Just then, brushing the wind from the pines, the exquisite sound of a koto rose from a room on the second floor. The newly come guest in the detached room inclined his ear.
takes.label: Drier social satire
takes.line: Narration plainer and more ironic, the scenic passages kept but tightened, the comedy of rank, antiques and fees allowed to sound almost dry. Tatsuya becomes a superior operator among operators; Zenpei funnier and more nakedly acquisitive; Tsunao’s stiffness more obviously a social defect. This gains speed and bite, but risks losing the genuine sensuous attraction of the hot-spring world and turning Mitsuyo’s danger into an epigram. Wrong for it: contemporary bureaucratic jargon or satire so broad that Zenpei ceases to be a doting father.

english: The wild bush-clover fawning upon the wattle fence, the dew beneath it already wears the colour of autumn. People vie with one another to hasten home. Upstairs and down, the Umeya, which holds the first place for beauty among the hot springs of Komatsu and was lately so thronged with merry company, now, moved to sorrow by the deer-whistles sounding across the ridge, hears the footsteps passing in its corridors grown somewhat lonely. Carriage after carriage, most of them laden with travelling bags and guests, runs toward the station a ri ahead. The maids, long grown familiar and close through the carrying of trays and the carrying of tea, stand a while even so to watch the departing figures away. The mountain stream circling before it flows on afar with a murmuring rush. Is it a thrush that sings in the forest yonder?

Even in these mountains, where morning and evening sustenance was once unknown, the summer guests of each year have added unlooked-for smoke, and tiled roofs show here and there through the leaves. There is cloud upon the ridge, rising from the roots of one towering pine to trail over the ivy tangled upon the rocks. The serried peaks hide the sky of the market town, and the thousand streaks of falling cataracts toss about like tangled threads of silver. To the north, as far as the eye can reach, the deer-fences stand stark and the clappers run far in line, and the autumn in the mountain paddies looks busy. To the west the water shows its far destination, mountains upon mountains and clouds upon clouds, birds fly high and the leaves turn of themselves. One or two grass-cutting children, rich at heart, walking their horses and singing a merry tune in turn, are now climbing the skirts of the outer mountain.

The waves of Lake Ogi are utterly still. The shadow of a leaf-boat coaxed by storm, slipping behind an island, faintly shows. Just then, brushing aside the wind in the pines, the exquisite sound of a koto rose from a room on the second floor. The newly come guest of the detached parlour bent his ear to listen.
takes.label: Fuller Meiji melodrama
takes.line: Narration more formal and emotionally open, with the lake, music and first sight of Mitsuyo given romantic amplitude. Tatsuya is smoother and more dangerous, Tsunao more evidently the honourable lover, Mitsuyo more lyrical and imperilled. This is playable and may suit serial publication, but it is the riskiest take: it can settle ambiguities the story withholds and make Tatsuya’s late demand feel like a villain’s unmasking rather than the logical price of everything before it. Wrong for it: fainting innocence, Byronic darkness, or consolation at the close.
